title: Φύζα Ἀχαιῶν
about: Night comes on the Achaean camp with panic among the chiefs, and Agamemnon calls an assembly in tears. He repeats the words of his old trial of the army, that Zeus has deceived him and they must sail home, and the army sits silent. Diomedes rebukes him: the king may go if he wishes, but he and Sthenelus will fight on until Troy falls, and the army cheers. Nestor praises Diomedes and proposes a meal and a night guard at the ditch; seven captains, each with a hundred men, take their posts between the ditch and the wall. At the feast in Agamemnon's hut Nestor begins to speak: he reminds the king of the wrong done to Achilles and urges that they try to win him back with gifts and gentle words.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν Τρῶες φυλακὰς ἔχον·
sentences.l: So they, on the one hand, the Trojans, were holding watches;
sentences.i: So the Trojans, for their part, kept their watches;
sentences.n: Book 9 opens by turning from the Trojans, whose watchfires close Book 8, to the Achaeans. ὣς οἱ μὲν Τρῶες is ‘so they, the Trojans’, where οἱ is the article used as a pronoun and μέν ‘on the one hand’ waits for the αὐτάρ ‘but’ of the next unit. φυλακὰς ἔχον is ‘were holding watches’; ἔχον is an imperfect without the augment (Attic εἶχον).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὺς
θεσπεσίη ἔχε φύζα φόβου κρυόεντος ἑταίρη,
πένθεϊ δ’ ἀτλήτῳ βεβολήατο πάντες ἄριστοι.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
wondrous panic held, companion of chilling terror,
and with unendurable grief were struck all the best.
sentences.i: but a wondrous panic, companion of chilling terror, held the Achaeans, and all their best men were struck with unendurable grief.
sentences.n: Panic is spoken of as a power that seizes an army: φύζα ‘panic’ is the subject of ἔχε ‘held’ (an imperfect without the augment) and Ἀχαιούς its object. φόβου κρυόεντος ἑταίρη is ‘companion of chilling terror’, ἑταίρη being the feminine of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’; φόβος can also mean flight itself. θεσπεσίη is ‘wondrous’. βεβολήατο is the pluperfect passive of βάλλω ‘strike’, with the epic ending -ήατο (Attic -ηντο), here ‘were struck’; πάντες ἄριστοι is ‘all the best men’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ἄνεμοι δύο πόντον ὀρίνετον ἰχθυόεντα
Βορέης καὶ Ζέφυρος, τώ τε Θρῄκηθεν ἄητον
ἐλθόντ’ ἐξαπίνης·
sentences.i: As when two winds, the North Wind and the West Wind, stir up the fish-teeming sea, the two that blow from Thrace, coming on suddenly;
sentences.n: A simile begins and runs to the end of line 8. ὀρίνετον, ἄητον and ἐλθόντ’ are duals, the forms for a pair: ‘the two stir up’, ‘the two blow’, ‘having come’; ὀρίνω is ‘stir up’, ἄημι ‘blow’, and τώ is ‘which two’. Βορέης is the North Wind and Ζέφυρος the West Wind, and Θρῄκηθεν is ‘from Thrace’ (the suffix -θεν means ‘from’). Line 5 is metrically irregular as transmitted: Βορέης has to be read with its first syllable counted long and its -εη- run together, and the short τε before Θρῄκηθεν has to be counted long, in the fourth foot.

sentences.t:
ἄμυδις δέ τε κῦμα κελαινὸν
κορθύεται, πολλὸν δὲ παρὲξ ἅλα φῦκος ἔχευεν·
sentences.l:
and at once a dark wave
rears itself up, and much seaweed out beyond the salt-sea it has poured;
sentences.i: and at once a dark wave rears itself up and pours much seaweed out beyond the sea;
sentences.n: The sea driven by the two winds. ἄμυδις ‘at once’ with δέ τε links the wave to the winds; κορθύεται, a present middle, is ‘rears itself up’, said of a wave rising to a crest, and κελαινόν is ‘dark’. ἔχευεν is an aorist of χέω ‘pour’, but a simile says what happens every time, so the free English uses the present. παρὲξ ἅλα is ‘out beyond the salt-sea’, onto the shore, and φῦκος is ‘seaweed’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐδαΐζετο θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: So was torn the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans was torn apart.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ ends the simile: the army’s heart is the stirred-up sea. ἐδαΐζετο is the imperfect passive of δαΐζω ‘tear apart’. θυμός ‘heart’ is singular because the poet speaks of one feeling shared by all; ἐνὶ is ἐν ‘in’, and στήθεσσιν is the epic dative plural of στῆθος ‘breast’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἄχεϊ μεγάλῳ βεβολημένος ἦτορ
φοίτα κηρύκεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισι κελεύων
κλήδην εἰς ἀγορὴν κικλήσκειν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον,
μὴ δὲ βοᾶν·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son, with great grief struck in heart,
went to and fro, the clear-voiced heralds bidding
by name to assembly to summon each man,
and not to shout;
sentences.i: And the son of Atreus, his heart struck with great grief, went to and fro, bidding the clear-voiced heralds to summon each man by name to the assembly, and not to shout;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is Agamemnon, and the edition’s paragraph break marks the turn to him. βεβολημένος is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω ‘struck’, with ἦτορ ‘heart’ in the accusative to say where. κελεύων ‘bidding’ takes the dative κηρύκεσσι and two infinitives, κικλήσκειν ‘to summon’ and βοᾶν ‘to shout’; κλήδην is ‘by name’, so the heralds are to call each man in person and not cry a general summons. φοίτα is ‘went to and fro’.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δὲ μετὰ πρώτοισι πονεῖτο.
sentences.l: and himself among the first he toiled.
sentences.i: and he himself toiled among the first.
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘he himself’ is set against the heralds, who do the calling: the king shares the work. μετὰ πρώτοισι is ‘among the first’, with the dative plural, and πονεῖτο is the imperfect middle of πονέομαι ‘toil’, the verb used of Menelaus at 2.409.

sentences.t: ἷζον δ’ εἰν ἀγορῇ τετιηότες·
sentences.l: And they sat down in assembly, grieved;
sentences.i: And they sat down in the assembly, grieving;
sentences.n: The Achaeans take their seats. ἷζον is the imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit down’, ‘seated themselves’, and εἰν is the epic form of ἐν ‘in’. τετιηότες ‘grieved’ is a perfect participle, the active beside the middle τετιημένος; the root of the word is not known.

sentences.t:
ἂν δ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
ἵστατο δάκρυ χέων ὥς τε κρήνη μελάνυδρος
ἥ τε κατ’ αἰγίλιπος πέτρης δνοφερὸν χέει ὕδωρ·
sentences.i: and Agamemnon stood up, shedding tears, like a dark-watered spring that pours its gloomy water down a sheer rock;
sentences.n: ἂν δ’ … ἵστατο is ἀνίστατο ‘stood up’, the preverb ἀνά set apart from its verb (tmesis); δάκρυ χέων is ‘shedding tears’. His tears are compared to a μελάνυδρος ‘dark-watered’ spring pouring down a rock. αἰγίλιπος is uncertain in sense: ‘sheer’ is the usual guess, from αἴξ ‘goat’ and λείπω ‘leave’, a rock even goats leave. δνοφερόν is ‘gloomy’, and χέει the present of χέω ‘pour’ in its open epic form.

sentences.t: ὣς ὃ βαρὺ στενάχων ἔπε’ Ἀργείοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: So he, groaning heavily, among the Argives spoke words:
sentences.i: So, groaning heavily, he spoke words among the Argives:
sentences.n: ὣς ὃ ‘so he’ closes the simile and gives the speech to Agamemnon, in the whole-line formula that introduces it. βαρὺ στενάχων is ‘groaning heavily’; ἔπε’ is ἔπεα ‘words’, elided; Ἀργείοισι is the epic dative plural, ‘the Argives’, the poet’s name here for the army Agamemnon calls his own; μετηύδα is ‘spoke among’.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
Ζεύς με μέγα Κρονίδης ἄτῃ ἐνέδησε βαρείῃ
σχέτλιος, ὃς τότε μέν μοι ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσεν
Ἴλιον ἐκπέρσαντ’ εὐτείχεον ἀπονέεσθαι,
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
Zeus me greatly, the son-of-Cronus, in bewilderment has bound, heavy,
cruel one, who then indeed promised me and nodded assent
that Ilios, well-walled, having sacked-utterly, I should return home;
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives: Zeus, the son of Cronus, has bound me hard in heavy bewilderment — cruel one that he is, who at that time promised me, and pledged it with a nod, that I should sack well-walled Ilios and return home;
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s speech, 9.17–28, repeats much of what he said at 2.110–141, where proposing flight was a trick to test the army; here nothing says it is a test. The first address is the one Nestor used at 2.79. ἐνέδησε is the aorist of ἐνδέω ‘bind’, ἄτῃ βαρείῃ ‘in heavy bewilderment’ (ἄτη, the blind folly a god sends), and σχέτλιος ‘cruel one’ stands beside Ζεύς. τότε μέν ‘at that time’ is answered by νῦν δέ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ κακὴν ἀπάτην βουλεύσατο, καί με κελεύει
δυσκλέα Ἄργος ἱκέσθαι, ἐπεὶ πολὺν ὤλεσα λαόν.
sentences.l:
but now an evil deceit he has devised, and bids me
inglorious to Argos to come, since a great host I have lost.
sentences.i: but now he has devised an evil deceit, and bids me return to Argos without glory, since I have lost so many of my people.
sentences.n: The turn from promise to deceit. ἀπάτην is ‘deceit’ and βουλεύσατο ‘has devised’, the aorist middle of βουλεύω; κελεύει ‘bids’ takes με and the infinitive ἱκέσθαι ‘to come’, with Ἄργος ‘Argos’ as the goal, the home country. δυσκλέα ‘inglorious’ agrees with με. The reason is ἐπεὶ πολὺν ὤλεσα λαόν, ‘since I have lost a great host’, ὤλεσα being the aorist of ὄλλυμι.

sentences.t:
οὕτω που Διὶ μέλλει ὑπερμενέϊ φίλον εἶναι,
ὃς δὴ πολλάων πολίων κατέλυσε κάρηνα
ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ λύσει·
sentences.i: So, I suppose, it is bound to be dear to Zeus of surpassing strength, who has overthrown the heads of many cities and will overthrow more;
sentences.n: Agamemnon puts the blame on the will of Zeus. οὕτω που is ‘so, I suppose’; μέλλει with the infinitive εἶναι is ‘is likely to be’, and φίλον ‘dear’ goes with the dative Διὶ ὑπερμενέϊ, ‘to Zeus of surpassing strength’. κατέλυσε is the aorist of καταλύω ‘undo, overthrow’ and λύσει its future; κάρηνα ‘heads’ is a figure for the cities, and the Greek does not say which part.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον.
sentences.l: for of him the strength is greatest.
sentences.i: for his strength is greatest.
sentences.n: The reason Zeus can do this. τοῦ is the demonstrative ‘of him’, Zeus, and κράτος ‘strength’ is the subject, with μέγιστον ‘greatest’ as its predicate. Diomedes picks the same words up at 39.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες·
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: The proposal opens. ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ is ‘but come’, the plural of ἄγε with its ending cut; ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω is ‘as I may say’, a clause of manner with the subjunctive, and πειθώμεθα ‘let us obey’ is a subjunctive of urging from πείθομαι. πάντες ‘all of us’ agrees with the subject.

sentences.t: φεύγωμεν σὺν νηυσὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.l: Let us flee with the ships to our dear fatherland;
sentences.i: let us flee with our ships to our dear fatherland;
sentences.n: The plan itself. φεύγωμεν is a subjunctive of urging, ‘let us flee’, with σὺν νηυσί ‘with the ships’; φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is the stock phrase ‘to the dear fatherland’, and Diomedes will give it back to him at 47.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔτι Τροίην αἱρήσομεν εὐρυάγυιαν.
sentences.l: for no longer shall we take Troy, wide-streeted.”
sentences.i: for we shall no longer take Troy of the wide streets.”
sentences.n: The reason for flight. αἱρήσομεν is the future of αἱρέω ‘take’, here a city, and Τροίην is ‘Troy’; εὐρυάγυιαν ‘wide-streeted’ (εὐρύς ‘wide’ and ἀγυιά ‘street’) is its stock epithet. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: The reaction to the speech. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’, the formula that closes a speech, and the edition’s paragraph begins here. ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is ‘they became still in silence’: ἀκήν is an adverb ‘in stillness’, and σιωπῇ is the dative of σιωπή ‘silence’.

sentences.t: δὴν δ’ ἄνεῳ ἦσαν τετιηότες υἷες Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l: For a long while speechless they were, grieved, the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: For a long time the sons of the Achaeans were speechless, grieving;
sentences.n: The silence lasts. δήν is ‘for a long time’, and ἄνεῳ ἦσαν ‘they were speechless’ (the adjective ἄνεως, in the nominative plural) is the same state as ἄνεῳ ἐγένοντο at 3.84. τετιηότες ‘grieved’ is the participle of line 13, and υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ is the stock phrase for the army.

sentences.t: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.l: But late indeed spoke among them Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: At last Diomedes, good at the war-cry, spoke among them:
sentences.n: Diomedes breaks the silence. ὀψὲ δὲ δή is ‘but late indeed’, which in English is ‘at last’; μετέειπε is the aorist of μεταείπον ‘spoke among’, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is his stock epithet, with βοήν in the accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη σοὶ πρῶτα μαχήσομαι ἀφραδέοντι,
ἣ θέμις ἐστὶν ἄναξ ἀγορῇ·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, with you first I shall fight, you being senseless,
as is the custom, lord, in assembly;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, with you I shall fight first, when you are senseless, as is the custom, lord, in the assembly;
sentences.n: Diomedes answers Agamemnon’s taunt at 4.370 ff, and he says at once that he is within his rights. μαχήσομαι is the future middle of μάχομαι ‘fight’, here a fight in words; ἀφραδέοντι is a participle in the dative agreeing with σοί, ‘you being senseless’. ἣ θέμις ἐστίν is the stock ‘as is the custom’, and ἄναξ is the vocative ‘lord’; ἀγορῇ ‘in assembly’ is a dative of place.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ μή τι χολωθῇς.
sentences.l: but you, do not at all become angered.
sentences.i: but do not be angry at all.
sentences.n: A courteous request. χολωθῇς is the aorist passive subjunctive of χολόομαι ‘be angered’ (from χόλος ‘anger’), which with μή forms a prohibition, and μή τι is ‘not at all’.

sentences.t:
ἀλκὴν μέν μοι πρῶτον ὀνείδισας ἐν Δαναοῖσι
φὰς ἔμεν ἀπτόλεμον καὶ ἀνάλκιδα·
sentences.l:
My might, indeed, first of all you reproached among the Danaans,
saying that I am unwarlike and without might;
sentences.i: First of all you reproached my might among the Danaans, saying that I am unwarlike and without might;
sentences.n: Diomedes recalls Agamemnon’s rebuke in Book 4. ἀλκήν ‘might’ is what was reproached, with ὀνείδισας ‘you reproached’ the aorist of ὀνειδίζω. φάς is the aorist participle of φημί ‘saying’, with ἔμεν (= εἶναι) ‘that I am’. ἀπτόλεμον ‘unwarlike’ and ἀνάλκιδα ‘without might’ (ἀ- and ἀλκή) pick up ἀλκήν, so the charge is cowardice; ἐν Δαναοῖσι is ‘among the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δὲ πάντα
ἴσασ’ Ἀργείων ἠμὲν νέοι ἠδὲ γέροντες.
sentences.l:
and all this
know of the Argives both young men and old.
sentences.i: and all this the Argives know, both the young and the old.
sentences.n: Diomedes calls the whole army to witness. ἴσασ’ is ἴσασι, the third plural of οἶδα ‘know’, with ταῦτα πάντα ‘all this’ as object; Ἀργείων is a partitive genitive with νέοι ‘young men’ and γέροντες ‘old men’, and ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’.

sentences.t: σοὶ δὲ διάνδιχα δῶκε Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω·
sentences.l: but to you in two ways gave the son of Cronus, of crooked cunning;
sentences.i: But the son of Cronus, of crooked cunning, gave to you in two ways:
sentences.n: The next two lines say what the two ways are. διάνδιχα is ‘in two ways’, the word used at 1.189 of Achilles’ two minds, and δῶκε is the aorist of δίδωμι without the augment. Κρόνου πάϊς is ‘the son of Cronus’ (πάϊς is the epic form of παῖς), Zeus, with ἀγκυλομήτεω ‘of crooked cunning’ as his stock epithet (epic genitive -εω).

sentences.t:
σκήπτρῳ μέν τοι δῶκε τετιμῆσθαι περὶ πάντων,
ἀλκὴν δ’ οὔ τοι δῶκεν, ὅ τε κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον.
sentences.l:
with a sceptre, indeed, he gave you to be honoured above all,
but might he did not give you, which is the greatest strength.
sentences.i: He gave you to be honoured above all with a sceptre, but he did not give you might, and that is the greatest strength.
sentences.n: The two gifts. σκήπτρῳ μέν ‘with a sceptre, on the one hand’ is answered by ἀλκὴν δ’ ‘but might’; τετιμῆσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of τιμάω ‘to be honoured’, after δῶκε, and περὶ πάντων is ‘above all’. The relative ὅ τε κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον is neuter because it agrees with κράτος ‘strength’; it turns Agamemnon’s own words at 25 about Zeus against him.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’ οὕτω που μάλα ἔλπεαι υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
ἀπτολέμους τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ ἀνάλκιδας ὡς ἀγορεύεις;
sentences.l:
Strange man, so, I suppose, you greatly expect the sons of the Achaeans
to be unwarlike and without might, as you declare?
sentences.i: Strange man, do you, then, really expect the sons of the Achaeans to be unwarlike and without might, as you declare?
sentences.n: A question, marked in the edition by the Greek semicolon. δαιμόνι’, the vocative of δαιμόνιος, is ‘strange man’: half reproach, said to someone behaving oddly. ἔλπεαι is the second singular of ἔλπομαι ‘expect’ in its open epic form, ἔμεναι (= εἶναι) the infinitive ‘to be’, and ὡς ἀγορεύεις ‘as you declare’ refers to Agamemnon’s public words. που ‘I suppose’ lends a touch of irony; ἀπτολέμους and ἀνάλκιδας repeat his insult.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τοι αὐτῷ θυμὸς ἐπέσσυται ὥς τε νέεσθαι
ἔρχεο·
sentences.l:
But if to you yourself your heart is driven so as to go home,
go;
sentences.i: But if your own heart is set on going home, go;
sentences.n: Diomedes takes Agamemnon at his word. The condition has an imperative for its answer: ‘if your heart is set on going, go’. ἐπέσσυται is the perfect passive of ἐπισεύω, ‘is driven, is set on’, with τοι (= σοι) and αὐτῷ ‘you yourself’; ὥς τε νέεσθαι is ‘so as to go home’ (νέομαι ‘go back’), and ἔρχεο is the imperative middle of ἔρχομαι.

sentences.t:
πάρ τοι ὁδός, νῆες δέ τοι ἄγχι θαλάσσης
ἑστᾶσ’, αἵ τοι ἕποντο Μυκήνηθεν μάλα πολλαί.
sentences.l:
the way is at hand for you, and your ships, near the sea,
stand, which followed you from Mycenae, very many.
sentences.i: the road is at hand for you, and your ships stand near the sea, the ones that followed you from Mycenae in great numbers.
sentences.n: Nothing hinders him from leaving. πάρ is πάρα ‘is at hand’, so πάρ τοι ὁδός is ‘there is a road for you’, and τοι is σοι ‘for you’, ‘your’. ἑστᾶσ’ is ἑστᾶσι, the third plural perfect of ἵστημι, ‘stand’. Μυκήνηθεν is ‘from Mycenae’, Agamemnon’s own city, and αἵ … μάλα πολλαί ‘very many of them’ describes the ships that followed him.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄλλοι μενέουσι κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
εἰς ὅ κέ περ Τροίην διαπέρσομεν.
sentences.l:
But the others will stay, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
until we sack Troy.
sentences.i: But the others will stay, the long-haired Achaeans, until we sack Troy.
sentences.n: ἄλλοι ‘the others’ means every other Achaean. μενέουσι is the future of μένω ‘stay’ in its open epic form, and κάρη κομόωντες, literally ‘wearing the hair long on the head’, is the stock ‘long-haired’. εἰς ὅ κέ περ … διαπέρσομεν is ‘until we sack’: διαπέρσομεν is an aorist subjunctive with the short vowel, used with κε, and διαπέρθω keeps the house ‘sack’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
φευγόντων σὺν νηυσὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.l:
But if they too, themselves,
let them flee with the ships to their dear fatherland;
sentences.i: But if they themselves also want to, let them flee with their ships to their dear fatherland;
sentences.n: Diomedes returns Agamemnon’s own plan to him: line 47 is line 27 with the verb in the third person. The ‘if’ clause has no verb in the Greek, which goes straight to the answer, so ‘want to’ is supplied in the English. εἰ δὲ καὶ αὐτοί is ‘but if they themselves too’, and φευγόντων is the third plural present imperative ‘let them flee’.

sentences.t:
νῶϊ δ’ ἐγὼ Σθένελός τε μαχησόμεθ’ εἰς ὅ κε τέκμωρ
Ἰλίου εὕρωμεν·
sentences.l:
But we two, I and Sthenelus, will fight until an end
of Ilios we find;
sentences.i: But the two of us, I and Sthenelus, will fight until we find an end for Ilios;
sentences.n: Diomedes and his companion Sthenelus will stay. νῶϊ is the dual pronoun ‘we two’, in apposition to ἐγώ and Σθένελος; μαχησόμεθ’ is the future middle ‘we shall fight’. εἰς ὅ κε … εὕρωμεν is ‘until we find’, an aorist subjunctive with κε, and τέκμωρ is an ‘end’, the goal reached, as in the same words at 7.30.

sentences.t: σὺν γὰρ θεῷ εἰλήλουθμεν.
sentences.l: for with a god we have come.”
sentences.i: for it is with a god that we have come.”
sentences.n: The reason Diomedes will not leave. σὺν … θεῷ ‘with a god’ has no article and does not say which god. εἰλήλουθμεν is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘we have come’ (so ‘we are here’), in the Homeric form with the lengthened reduplication εἰ- and the ending -μεν. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπίαχον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
μῦθον ἀγασσάμενοι Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all shouted, the sons of the Achaeans,
in admiration at the word of Diomedes, horse-taming;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all the sons of the Achaeans shouted in admiration at the word of Diomedes, tamer of horses;
sentences.n: The army approves Diomedes. ἐπίαχον is ‘shouted in response’ (a past tense of ἰάχω ‘cry out’ with the preverb ἐπί), υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ the subject, and ἀγασσάμενοι the aorist participle of ἀγάομαι, ‘in admiration’, which takes the accusative μῦθον ‘word’. Διομήδεος is the epic genitive of Διομήδης, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’ his stock epithet.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δ’ ἀνιστάμενος μετεφώνεεν ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: and among them, standing up, spoke the horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: And among them the horseman Nestor rose and spoke:
sentences.n: Nestor speaks next. τοῖσι is the dative ‘among them’, ἀνιστάμενος the participle ‘standing up’, and μετεφώνεεν the imperfect of μεταφωνέω ‘speak among’, in its uncontracted form. ἱππότα is the epic nominative of ἱππότης, ‘horseman’, Nestor’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδη περὶ μὲν πολέμῳ ἔνι καρτερός ἐσσι,
καὶ βουλῇ μετὰ πάντας ὁμήλικας ἔπλευ ἄριστος.
sentences.l:
“Tydeus’-son, beyond others in war you are strong,
and in counsel among all those of your age you are best.
sentences.i: “Son of Tydeus, you are strong in war beyond others, and in counsel you are the best among all those of your own age.
sentences.n: Nestor’s first speech, 9.53–78, praises Diomedes and then gives the plan. Τυδεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Tydeus’; περί is an adverb, ‘beyond others’, and ἔνι is ἐν ‘in’ set after its noun. ἔπλευ is ἔπλεο, a Homeric second singular of πέλομαι, here ‘you are’; ὁμήλικας ‘those of the same age’ is the object of μετά ‘among’.

sentences.t:
οὔ τίς τοι τὸν μῦθον ὀνόσσεται ὅσσοι Ἀχαιοί,
οὐδὲ πάλιν ἐρέει·
sentences.l:
No one of them will find fault with your word, as many as are Achaeans,
nor will he speak against it;
sentences.i: No one of all the Achaeans will find fault with your word, or speak against it;
sentences.n: The Achaeans will accept what Diomedes has said. ὀνόσσεται comes from ὄνομαι ‘find fault with, scorn’, and takes τὸν μῦθον ‘the word’; τοι is σοι ‘your’. ὅσσοι Ἀχαιοί is ‘as many Achaeans as there are’, that is, all of them, and πάλιν ἐρέει is ‘will say back’, ‘will speak against it’, the uncontracted future of ἐρῶ.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ οὐ τέλος ἵκεο μύθων.
sentences.l: but you did not reach the end of words.
sentences.i: but you did not reach the end of your words.
sentences.n: A gentle correction: the speech was good, but Nestor thinks it incomplete. τέλος μύθων is ‘the end of words’, the point where speaking arrives at a result; the usual sense is that Diomedes has not yet said all that needs saying. ἵκεο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’ (second singular; Attic ἵκου).

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν καὶ νέος ἐσσί, ἐμὸς δέ κε καὶ πάϊς εἴης
ὁπλότατος γενεῆφιν·
sentences.l:
Truly you are young too, and my own son you might be as well,
the youngest in birth;
sentences.i: Truly, you are young, and you might be my own son, my youngest by birth;
sentences.n: Nestor teases Diomedes about his youth, with respect. ἦ μέν is ‘truly’; κε with the optative εἴης makes ‘you might be’, and ἐμὸς … πάϊς is ‘my own son’ (πάϊς is the epic form of παῖς). ὁπλότατος ‘youngest’ is the superlative beside ὁπλότερος ‘younger’, and γενεῆφιν has the old ending -φιν where Attic would use a plain dative: ‘by birth’. So Diomedes is young enough to be Nestor’s youngest son.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ πεπνυμένα βάζεις
Ἀργείων βασιλῆας, ἐπεὶ κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.l:
but prudent things you speak
to the kings of the Argives, since as is fitting you have spoken.
sentences.i: but you speak prudent words to the kings of the Argives, since you have spoken as is fitting.
sentences.n: He grants the point: Diomedes has spoken well. πεπνυμένα ‘prudent things’ is what βάζεις ‘you speak’ says, and βασιλῆας ‘kings’ (accusative plural, epic -ῆας) are the persons spoken to. κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘as is fitting’, ‘according to what is due’, and ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with its doubled ε.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐγών, ὃς σεῖο γεραίτερος εὔχομαι εἶναι,
ἐξείπω καὶ πάντα διίξομαι·
sentences.l:
But come, I, who than you older claim to be,
will speak out and go through everything;
sentences.i: But come, I, who claim to be older than you, will speak out and go through it all;
sentences.n: Nestor claims the right of age. ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ is ‘but come’, and εὔχομαι εἶναι ‘claim to be’ takes σεῖο, the epic genitive of σύ, ‘than you’, after γεραίτερος ‘older’. ἐξείπω is an aorist subjunctive of urging, ‘let me speak out’, and διίξομαι the future of διικνέομαι ‘go through’: he will say it all and leave nothing out.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κέ τίς μοι
μῦθον ἀτιμήσει’, οὐδὲ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.l:
and no one would dishonour for me
the word, not even lord Agamemnon.
sentences.i: and no one would dishonour my word, not even lord Agamemnon.
sentences.n: No one, not even the king, would brush his words aside. ἀτιμήσει’ is ἀτιμήσειε, an optative with κέ, ‘would dishonour’, from ἀτιμάω, the opposite of τιμάω ‘honour’; μοι ‘for me’ goes with μῦθον to give ‘my word’ in the free English. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘lord Agamemnon’.

sentences.t:
ἀφρήτωρ ἀθέμιστος ἀνέστιός ἐστιν ἐκεῖνος
ὃς πολέμου ἔραται ἐπιδημίου ὀκρυόεντος.
sentences.l:
Clanless, lawless, hearthless is that man
who loves war among his own people, chilling.
sentences.i: That man is clanless, lawless and hearthless who loves chilling war among his own people.
sentences.n: A sharp saying about civil strife; the Greek names no one. ἀφρήτωρ ἀθέμιστος ἀνέστιος are three adjectives, each beginning with ἀ- ‘without’: no φρήτρη ‘clan’, no θέμις ‘law, custom’, no ἑστία ‘hearth’. ἐπιδημίου, from δῆμος ‘people’, is ‘among the people at home’, so war within one’s own community; ὀκρυόεντος ‘chilling’ is a rare word given by the traditional gloss. ἔραται is the third singular of ἔραμαι ‘love’, with the genitive.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μὲν πειθώμεθα νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ
δόρπά τ’ ἐφοπλισόμεσθα·
sentences.l:
But truly now let us obey black night
and make ready our suppers;
sentences.i: But for now let us give way to dark night and make ready our suppers;
sentences.n: Nestor’s practical proposal: stop for the night and eat. ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ‘but indeed’ has ἤτοι printed as one word, as the edition does. πειθώμεθα is a subjunctive of urging from πείθομαι ‘obey’, and with the dative νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ ‘black night’ it means ‘give way to night’, as at 7.282. δόρπά is the plural of δόρπον ‘supper’; ἐφοπλισόμεσθα, from ἐφοπλίζω ‘make ready’, is a first-person plural middle that carries on the ‘let us’. The first line is Odyssey 12.291 word for word (printed ἦ τοι there), so its English is kept.

sentences.t:
φυλακτῆρες δὲ ἕκαστοι
λεξάσθων παρὰ τάφρον ὀρυκτὴν τείχεος ἐκτός.
sentences.l:
and let the sentries, each of them,
lay themselves down beside the ditch, the dug one, outside the wall.
sentences.i: and let the sentries, every one of them, lie down beside the dug ditch, outside the wall.
sentences.n: The sentries are to hold the ditch dug in Book 7 (7.440–441), outside the wall. φυλακτῆρες is ‘sentries’, with ἕκαστοι ‘each of them’ in the plural; λεξάσθων is the third plural aorist imperative middle of λέγω ‘lay’, so ‘let them lay themselves down’, that is, take their posts. ὀρυκτήν ‘dug’ follows τάφρον ‘ditch’, and τείχεος is the epic genitive of τεῖχος ‘wall’, with ἐκτός ‘outside’.

sentences.t: κούροισιν μὲν ταῦτ’ ἐπιτέλλομαι·
sentences.l: To the youths, indeed, these things I enjoin;
sentences.i: These are my orders to the young men;
sentences.n: Nestor gives the night’s orders, first to the young men and then, in the next unit, to the king. ἐπιτέλλομαι is ‘I enjoin’, and κούροισιν the epic dative plural of κοῦρος ‘young man’; μέν waits for αὐτάρ in the same line. The English is the Odyssey’s, for the same half-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
Ἀτρεΐδη σὺ μὲν ἄρχε·
sentences.l:
but afterwards
Atreus’-son, you, indeed, lead;
sentences.i: but then, son of Atreus, you take the lead;
sentences.n: Now the orders for the king. αὐτάρ ‘but’ answers the μέν of the unit before; Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’, and ἄρχε a present imperative ‘lead’. σὺ μέν ‘you, for your part’ is explained by the σὺ γάρ of the next unit.

sentences.t: σὺ γὰρ βασιλεύτατός ἐσσι.
sentences.l: for you are the most kingly.
sentences.i: for you are the most kingly.
sentences.n: The reason Agamemnon should lead. βασιλεύτατος is the superlative of βασιλεύς ‘king’ itself, ‘most of a king’, a rare form; ‘most kingly’ keeps both the noun and the superlative. ἐσσι is the epic form of εἶ ‘you are’.

sentences.t: δαίνυ δαῖτα γέρουσιν·
sentences.l: Give a feast to the elders;
sentences.i: give the elders a feast;
sentences.n: Nestor tells the king to entertain the council. δαίνυ is the present imperative of δαίνυμι ‘give a feast’, with δαῖτα ‘feast’ as its inner object (‘feast the elders with a feast’), and γέρουσιν is the dative plural of γέρων ‘elder’.

sentences.t: ἔοικέ τοι, οὔ τοι ἀεικές.
sentences.l: it is fitting for you, not unseemly for you.
sentences.i: it suits you, and it is nothing unseemly for you.
sentences.n: ἔοικε is the impersonal ‘it is fitting’ (a perfect with the force of a present), and τοι is σοι ‘for you’. οὔ τοι ἀεικές ‘not unseemly for you’ puts the same thing in the negative, which strengthens it; ἀεικές is the neuter of ἀεικής ‘unseemly’, with ‘is’ understood.

sentences.t:
πλεῖαί τοι οἴνου κλισίαι, τὸν νῆες Ἀχαιῶν
ἠμάτιαι Θρῄκηθεν ἐπ’ εὐρέα πόντον ἄγουσι·
sentences.l:
Full for you of wine are the huts, which the ships of the Achaeans
day by day from Thrace over the wide sea bring;
sentences.i: Your huts are full of wine, which the ships of the Achaeans bring every day from Thrace over the wide sea;
sentences.n: Why Agamemnon can feast them: wine arrives daily by ship. πλεῖαι … οἴνου is ‘full of wine’, the genitive saying what fills, with κλισίαι ‘huts’; τὸν is the old demonstrative used as the relative ‘which’. ἠμάτιαι ‘day by day’ agrees with νῆες ‘ships’; Θρῄκηθεν is ‘from Thrace’, as in line 5, and εὐρέα is an epic accusative of εὐρύς ‘wide’.

sentences.t: πᾶσά τοί ἐσθ’ ὑποδεξίη, πολέεσσι δ’ ἀνάσσεις.
sentences.l: Every means of entertaining is yours, and over many you are lord.
sentences.i: You have every means of entertaining, and you are lord over many.
sentences.n: The king has both the means and the duty of hospitality. πᾶσα … ὑποδεξίη is ‘all means of receiving guests’, a rare noun built on ὑποδέχομαι ‘receive’; it is the subject, with τοί (= σοι) ‘yours’ and ἐστί cut to ἐσθ’. πολέεσσι is the epic dative plural of πολύς, and ἀνάσσεις ‘you are lord’ is the verb from ἄναξ.

sentences.t:
πολλῶν δ’ ἀγρομένων τῷ πείσεαι ὅς κεν ἀρίστην
βουλὴν βουλεύσῃ·
sentences.l:
Of many assembled, him you will obey who the best
counsel may devise;
sentences.i: When many are gathered, you will obey the one who devises the best counsel;
sentences.n: The king should follow the best advice, from whoever gives it. πολλῶν ἀγρομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘many being gathered’ (ἀγρομένων is a short form of the participle of ἀγείρομαι ‘gather’), and τῷ ‘him’ is the demonstrative that ὅς κεν … βουλεύσῃ ‘whoever may devise’ describes, an aorist subjunctive with κε. πείσεαι is the future of πείθομαι ‘obey’, and βουλὴν βουλεύσῃ puts noun and verb of one root together.

sentences.t:
μάλα δὲ χρεὼ πάντας Ἀχαιοὺς
ἐσθλῆς καὶ πυκινῆς, ὅτι δήϊοι ἐγγύθι νηῶν
καίουσιν πυρὰ πολλά·
sentences.i: and all the Achaeans have great need of good and shrewd counsel, because the enemy are burning many fires near the ships;
sentences.n: Why counsel matters tonight. χρεώ ‘need’ takes the accusative of those in need, πάντας Ἀχαιούς, and the genitive of what is needed, ἐσθλῆς καὶ πυκινῆς ‘good and shrewd’, which agrees with a βουλῆς ‘counsel’ that the Greek leaves unsaid after βουλὴν βουλεύσῃ. δήϊοι is ‘enemies’, ἐγγύθι νηῶν ‘near the ships’, and καίουσιν πυρὰ πολλά ‘are burning many fires’: the Trojan fires of 8.553–565.

sentences.t: τίς ἂν τάδε γηθήσειε;
sentences.l: Who would rejoice at these things?
sentences.i: Who could be glad of this?
sentences.n: A question that answers itself: no one. τίς ἂν … γηθήσειε is an aorist optative with ἄν, ‘who would rejoice’, from γηθέω; τάδε ‘these things’ names what causes the joy, here the enemy fires of the clause before.

sentences.t: νὺξ δ’ ἧδ’ ἠὲ διαρραίσει στρατὸν ἠὲ σαώσει.
sentences.l: and this night will either shatter the army or save it.”
sentences.i: This night will either wreck the army or save it.”
sentences.n: Nestor’s first speech ends with the stakes. νὺξ δ’ ἧδ’ is ‘and this night’ (ἧδε ‘this’, elided); ἠέ … ἠέ is ‘either … or’, with two futures, διαρραίσει from διαρραίω ‘shatter, break up’ and σαώσει from σαόω ‘save’, and στρατόν ‘army’ is the object of both. He speaks again at 96.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδὲ πίθοντο.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed.
sentences.n: The elders accept the advice. The line is the same as 7.379 and Odyssey 13.477, which print ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο where this edition has ἠδὲ πίθοντο: the same words divided differently, so the English is theirs. κλύον is ‘heard’, with τοῦ ‘him’ in the genitive, and πίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθομαι ‘obey’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ φυλακτῆρες σὺν τεύχεσιν ἐσσεύοντο
ἀμφί τε Νεστορίδην Θρασυμήδεα ποιμένα λαῶν,
sentences.l:
And out the sentries with their arms rushed
around the son of Nestor, Thrasymedes, shepherd of the people,
sentences.i: Then the sentries rushed out with their arms, gathered about the son of Nestor, Thrasymedes, shepherd of the people,
sentences.n: The sentries form up under seven captains, named across this unit and the next. ἐκ … ἐσσεύοντο is ‘rushed out’: ἐκ is set apart from the verb (tmesis), and ἐσσεύοντο is the imperfect of σεύομαι ‘rush’ with a doubled σ. ἀμφί with the accusative is ‘about, around’: the men gather about their leader. Νεστορίδην is ‘the son of Nestor’, and ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ the stock phrase.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀσκάλαφον καὶ Ἰάλμενον υἷας Ἄρηος
ἀμφί τε Μηριόνην Ἀφαρῆά τε Δηΐπυρόν τε,
ἠδ’ ἀμφὶ Κρείοντος υἱὸν Λυκομήδεα δῖον.
sentences.l:
and around Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares,
and around Meriones and Aphareus and Deipyrus,
and around the son of Creon, Lycomedes, heavenly.
sentences.i: and about Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares, and about Meriones, Aphareus and Deipyrus, and about Lycomedes, the heavenly son of Creon.
sentences.n: The other six captains, who with Thrasymedes make the seven of line 85. Ascalaphus and Ialmenus, sons of Ares, led the men of Orchomenus (2.512). The structure is a run of ἀμφί ‘around’ with the accusative, joined by ἠδέ and τε ‘and’; υἷας Ἄρηος is ‘sons of Ares’ and υἱὸν Κρείοντος ‘son of Creon’. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἕπτ’ ἔσαν ἡγεμόνες φυλάκων, ἑκατὸν δὲ ἑκάστῳ
κοῦροι ἅμα στεῖχον δολίχ’ ἔγχεα χερσὶν ἔχοντες·
sentences.l:
Seven were the leaders of the guards, and a hundred to each
young men together went, long spears in their hands holding;
sentences.i: There were seven leaders of the guards, and a hundred young men went along with each, holding long spears in their hands;
sentences.n: Seven captains, a hundred men each: seven hundred in all. ἕπτ’ is ἑπτά ‘seven’ elided, and ἔσαν is the Homeric ‘they were’ (Attic ἦσαν); ἡγεμόνες φυλάκων is ‘leaders of the guards’. ἑκατὸν … ἑκάστῳ is ‘a hundred to each’, κοῦροι ‘young men’ is the subject of στεῖχον ‘went’, and δολίχ’ is δολιχά ‘long’; χερσὶν ἔχοντες ‘holding in their hands’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t: κὰδ δὲ μέσον τάφρου καὶ τείχεος ἷζον ἰόντες·
sentences.l: and down midway between the ditch and the wall they sat, going there;
sentences.i: and going there they sat down between the ditch and the wall;
sentences.n: κὰδ δὲ … ἷζον is καθῖζον ‘sat down’: κὰδ is κατά with its last vowel dropped and its τ made like the δ after it, and it stands apart from its verb (tmesis). μέσον is ‘midway’, an adverb with the genitives τάφρου καὶ τείχεος ‘between the ditch and the wall’, and ἰόντες is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’: they went there and sat. The ditch lay just outside the wall (7.440–441), so they sit in the strip between.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δὲ πῦρ κήαντο, τίθεντο δὲ δόρπα ἕκαστος.
sentences.l: and there they kindled a fire, and set out their suppers, each man.
sentences.i: and there they lit a fire, and each man prepared his supper.
sentences.n: The camp-fire of the watch. κήαντο is the aorist middle of καίω ‘burn’, without the augment: ‘they lit’. τίθεντο, the imperfect middle of τίθημι, with δόρπα ‘suppers’, is ‘they set out, prepared’; ἕκαστος ‘each man’ is singular though the verb is plural, a common way of saying that every one of them did it.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ γέροντας ἀολλέας ἦγεν Ἀχαιῶν
ἐς κλισίην, παρὰ δέ σφι τίθει μενοεικέα δαῖτα.
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son the elders, in a close mass, of the Achaeans led
to his hut, and beside them set a satisfying feast.
sentences.i: And the son of Atreus led the elders of the Achaeans, in a close mass, to his hut, and set before them a satisfying feast.
sentences.n: From the sentries the scene moves to the council in Agamemnon’s hut. Ἀτρεΐδης is Agamemnon again, and γέροντας Ἀχαιῶν ‘the elders of the Achaeans’ the object of ἦγεν ‘led’; ἀολλέας is ‘in a close mass’, as at 5.498. In παρὰ δέ σφι τίθει, παρά is set apart from τίθει ‘set’ (tmesis, an imperfect without the augment), so ‘set before them’, with σφι ‘them’; μενοεικέα ‘satisfying’ is the Odyssey’s word for what suits the heart.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: The formula for the start of a meal, also at Odyssey 1.149. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα ‘good things’ to eat, with ἑτοῖμα ‘ready’ and προκείμενα ‘lying before them’ agreeing; ἴαλλον is the imperfect of ἰάλλω ‘send’, so ‘they put out their hands’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖς ὁ γέρων πάμπρωτος ὑφαίνειν ἤρχετο μῆτιν
Νέστωρ, οὗ καὶ πρόσθεν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλή·
sentences.i: When they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the old man was the first of all to begin weaving a plan for them: Nestor, whose counsel had also seemed best before.
sentences.n: The feast ends and Nestor opens the council, in the same three lines as at 7.323–325. αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ … ἕντο is the formula for the end of a meal: ἕντο is the aorist middle of ἵημι ‘put away’, with ἔρον ‘desire’. ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, named only in line 94; ὑφαίνειν … μῆτιν ‘to weave a plan’ is a figure, and ἀρίστη … βουλή ‘best counsel’ with φαίνετο ‘appeared’ tells why he is trusted.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: The line that introduces Nestor’s second speech, the same as 7.326. ὅ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘he’, with σφιν ‘to them’; ἐϋφρονέων is a participle of ἐϋφρονέω ‘be kindly in mind’, ἀγορήσατο the aorist of ἀγοράομαι ‘address the assembly’, and μετέειπεν the aorist of μεταείπον ‘spoke among’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
ἐν σοὶ μὲν λήξω,
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
in you I shall end,
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, with you I shall end,
sentences.n: Nestor’s second speech, 9.96–113, starts here and ends with the last line of this part. The address is that of 2.434. κύδιστε is ‘most glorious’ and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’, both stock; ἐν σοὶ μὲν λήξω is ‘with you I shall end’, and the μέν looks forward to σέο δ’ ἄρξομαι ‘and from you I shall begin’ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
σέο δ’ ἄρξομαι, οὕνεκα πολλῶν
λαῶν ἐσσι ἄναξ καί τοι Ζεὺς ἐγγυάλιξε
σκῆπτρόν τ’ ἠδὲ θέμιστας, ἵνά σφισι βουλεύῃσθα.
sentences.l:
and from you I shall begin, because over many
people you are lord, and to you Zeus has put into your hands
the sceptre and the rules of right, that for them you may take counsel.
sentences.i: and from you I shall begin, because you are lord over many people, and Zeus has put into your hands the sceptre and the rules of right, so that you may take counsel for them.
sentences.n: Nestor will begin and end with the king, and he gives two reasons. ἄρξομαι is ‘I shall begin’, with the genitive σέο ‘from you’; οὕνεκα ‘because’ brings first that Agamemnon is ἄναξ ‘lord’ of many, and then that Zeus has put σκῆπτρον ‘the sceptre’ and θέμιστας ‘rules of right’ (the judgements and customs a king upholds) into his hands: ἐγγυάλιξε is the aorist of ἐγγυαλίζω. ἵνα … βουλεύῃσθα is a purpose clause with the subjunctive, and σφισι is ‘for them’.

sentences.t:
τώ σε χρὴ περὶ μὲν φάσθαι ἔπος ἠδ’ ἐπακοῦσαι,
κρηῆναι δὲ καὶ ἄλλῳ,
sentences.l:
Therefore you must above all speak a word and listen,
and bring to fulfilment for another also,
sentences.i: So you above all must speak a word and listen, and bring to fulfilment for another man as well,
sentences.n: What a king must do. τώ is τῷ ‘therefore’, and χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes σε and three infinitives: φάσθαι ‘to speak’, ἐπακοῦσαι ‘to listen’, and κρηῆναι ‘to bring to fulfilment’, the aorist of κραίνω, the verb behind ἐπεκραίαινε at 2.419. περὶ μέν is ‘above all’. κρηῆναι has no object in the Greek: it is what another man proposes, as the next unit says, and ἄλλῳ is ‘for another’.

sentences.t:
ὅτ’ ἄν τινα θυμὸς ἀνώγῃ
εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν·
sentences.l:
whenever any man the heart bids
to speak for good;
sentences.i: whenever a man’s heart bids him speak for good;
sentences.n: ὅτ’ ἄν … ἀνώγῃ is ‘whenever … bids’, ὅτε with ἄν and the subjunctive of ἄνωγα ‘I bid’ (a perfect used as a present); θυμός ‘heart’ is the subject and τινα ‘any man’ the object. εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν is ‘to speak for good’, that is, to a good end.

sentences.t: σέο δ’ ἕξεται ὅττί κεν ἄρχῃ.
sentences.l: and on you will rest whatever he may begin.
sentences.i: and whatever he begins will rest with you.
sentences.n: The king decides whether a good proposal is carried out. σέο … ἕξεται is the future middle of ἔχω with the genitive, ‘will hold on to you, will depend on you’, with σέο the epic genitive of σύ. ὅττί κεν ἄρχῃ is ‘whatever he may begin’: ὅττι is ὅ τι ‘whatever’, and ἄρχῃ is the subjunctive of ἄρχω ‘begin’, here ‘put forward’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐρέω ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα.
sentences.l: But I shall say as it seems to me to be best.
sentences.i: But I will say it as it seems best to me.
sentences.n: Nestor turns to his own counsel. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ, and ἐρέω is the uncontracted future of ἐρῶ ‘I shall say’. ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα is ‘as it seems to me to be best’, with ἄριστα the neuter plural used as a superlative.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις νόον ἄλλος ἀμείνονα τοῦδε νοήσει
οἷον ἐγὼ νοέω ἠμὲν πάλαι ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν
ἐξ ἔτι τοῦ ὅτε διογενὲς Βρισηΐδα κούρην
χωομένου Ἀχιλῆος ἔβης κλισίηθεν ἀπούρας
οὔ τι καθ’ ἡμέτερόν γε νόον·
sentences.i: For no one else will think of a better thought than this, such as I have in mind, both long ago and still even now, ever since the time, Zeus-born one, when you took the girl Briseis and went from his hut while Achilles was incensed, not at all according to our mind;
sentences.n: Nestor goes to the cause of the disaster: the taking of Briseis in Book 1. νόον ἀμείνονα τοῦδε is ‘a better thought than this’, τοῦδε being a genitive of comparison, and οἷον ἐγὼ νοέω ‘such as I think’; ἠμὲν πάλαι ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν ‘both long ago and still now’ says the plan is an old one. διογενές is ‘Zeus-born’, the address to Agamemnon; χωομένου Ἀχιλῆος is a genitive absolute, ‘Achilles being incensed’, and ἀπούρας the aorist participle of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’.

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ τοι ἔγωγε
πόλλ’ ἀπεμυθεόμην·
sentences.l:
for I, for my part, to you very much
spoke against it;
sentences.i: for I for my part argued against it with you again and again;
sentences.n: Nestor reminds him that he warned him (1.275–284). ἀπεμυθεόμην is the imperfect middle of ἀπομυθέομαι ‘speak against, advise against’, and an imperfect for repeated speaking is ‘again and again’; the Greek gives no object, so ‘it’ is the taking of the girl. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, ἔγωγε ‘I, for my part’, and μάλα … πόλλ’ ‘very much’ (πολλά used as an adverb).

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ σῷ μεγαλήτορι θυμῷ
εἴξας ἄνδρα φέριστον, ὃν ἀθάνατοί περ ἔτισαν,
ἠτίμησας,
sentences.l:
but you, to your great-spirited heart
having yielded, a man the best, whom the immortals even honoured,
dishonoured,
sentences.i: but you, yielding to your great-spirited heart, dishonoured a man who is the best, one whom even the immortals honoured,
sentences.n: The charge: Agamemnon let his pride rule him. εἴξας is the aorist participle of εἴκω ‘yield’, with the dative θυμῷ, and μεγαλήτορι is ‘great-spirited’. The man he wronged is ἄνδρα φέριστον ‘a man the best’, Achilles, not named here; ὃν ἀθάνατοί περ ἔτισαν is ‘whom even the immortals honoured’ (ἔτισαν, aorist of τίω), and the verb ἠτίμησας ‘you dishonoured’ is held to the end.

sentences.t: ἑλὼν γὰρ ἔχεις γέρας·
sentences.l: for having taken it, you hold the prize;
sentences.i: for you took the prize of honour and you keep it;
sentences.n: The wrong stated. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω ‘take’, ἔχεις ‘you hold’, and γέρας ‘prize of honour’ is the prize a chief receives: Briseis. Achilles used the same words of Agamemnon at 1.356, with ἔχει ‘he holds’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν
φραζώμεσθ’ ὥς κέν μιν ἀρεσσάμενοι πεπίθωμεν
δώροισίν τ’ ἀγανοῖσιν ἔπεσσί τε μειλιχίοισι.
sentences.l:
But even now still
let us consider how, having made him content, we may persuade him
with gentle gifts and with words, gentle ones.”
sentences.i: But even now let us consider how we may make him content and persuade him with gentle gifts and gentle words.”
sentences.n: Nestor’s proposal at last, and the end of his speech: Agamemnon answers at 114. φραζώμεσθ’ is a subjunctive of urging, ‘let us consider’, with ὥς κέν … πεπίθωμεν ‘how we may persuade’ (a reduplicated aorist subjunctive of πείθω); ἀρεσσάμενοι ‘having made him content’ comes from ἀρέσκω ‘please, satisfy’. ἀγανοῖσιν and μειλιχίοισι are two words that the house renderings both give as ‘gentle’, so ‘gentle’ stands twice.
